name: Ulnar approach to the hook of hamate
corridor: Ulnar palmar exposure through Guyon-canal territory with direct identification and mobilization of the ulnar nerve and artery to the hamate hook

positioning.text: Position supine with the forearm supinated on a hand table and the wrist gently extended and radially deviated to expose the ulnar palm.

setup.text: Prepare the hand and distal forearm, confirm the target on CT or appropriate imaging, and have microsurgical instruments available for ulnar neurovascular dissection.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark FCU, pisiform, palpable ulnar artery radial to FCU, hamate hook distal-radial to the pisiform, DRUJ level, and distal palmar crease.

incision.text: Use an approximately 5-cm zigzag incision beginning radial to FCU at DRUJ level, turning near the pisiform and distal palmar crease, then continuing distally in the hypothenar palm.

superficial_interval.text: Open antebrachial fascia proximally, identify the ulnar artery and nerve before entering Guyon canal, and divide palmaris brevis distally under direct vision.

deep_interval.text: Trace and protect the ulnar neurovascular bundle distally, retract it ulnarly, divide hypothenar origins from the hook as needed, and expose the hook subperiosteally.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, antebrachial fascia and palmaris brevis, Guyon canal with ulnar nerve and artery, hypothenar origins and pisohamate ligament, then hamate hook periosteum.

structures_encountered.text: FCU, pisiform, ulnar artery and nerve, superficial and deep ulnar branches, palmaris brevis, pisohamate ligament, flexor retinaculum, hypothenar origins, flexor tendons, and hamate hook are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: The ulnar artery, superficial sensory and deep motor branches of the ulnar nerve, superficial palmar arch, flexor tendons, and motor branches to hypothenar muscles are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The deep motor branch curves around the hook and the superficial palmar arch lies nearby; identify neurovascular anatomy before circumferential hook dissection or fragment removal.

retraction_hazards.text: Use gentle intermittent ulnar retraction of the nerve and artery and avoid traction transmitted to the deep motor branch around the hook.

exposure.text: Provides direct circumferential access to the hook for fragment excision or fixation and can be extended to selected pisiform excision or ulnar-tunnel decompression.

limitations.text: The approach places the ulnar neurovascular bundle directly in the operative field; excision changes ligament and hypothenar attachments and is not automatically preferable to fixation in every patient.

extensions.text: Extend proximally for Guyon-canal decompression or toward the pisiform for post-traumatic pisiform excision while maintaining direct control of ulnar nerve branches.

indications.text: Use for symptomatic displaced hook fractures, painful hook nonunion, fragment excision in selected athletes, ORIF in selected reconstructable fractures, and selected post-traumatic pisiform sequelae.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid fragment excision when preservation of hook biomechanics is prioritized and stable fixation is feasible; reassess the plan when ulnar neurovascular scarring makes safe mobilization uncertain.

implant_implications.text: For ORIF, choose a trajectory that captures the hook without entering adjacent joints or impinging the ulnar nerve or flexor tendons; after excision, remove all sharp residual prominence.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use dedicated carpal-tunnel or tangential views to localize the hook, verify complete excision or reduction, and confirm safe fixation when screws are used.

closure.text: Confirm intact ulnar-nerve branches and flexor glide, repair divided hypothenar fascia as appropriate without recreating compression, and close the zigzag skin incision without tension.

complications.text: Complications include transient or permanent ulnar sensory or motor dysfunction, vascular injury, scar pain, residual fragment pain, flexor-tendon irritation, weakness, infection, and reoperation.

bailouts.text: If scar or variant anatomy prevents safe hook access, extend Guyon-canal exposure and identify both superficial and deep ulnar branches before proceeding; do not remove the fragment blindly.

procedure_applications.condition: A symptomatic hook fracture or nonunion requires excision or fixation, or selected pisiform pathology requires excision

questions.question: What forms the borders of Guyon canal at the hamate level?
questions.answer: The pisiform medially and hook of hamate laterally; the canal contains the ulnar nerve and artery.

questions.question: Which ulnar-nerve branch is especially vulnerable around the hook?
Which muscles originate from the hook and may require release?
questions.answer: Flexor digiti minimi brevis and opponens digiti minimi.
